Born on 26 August 1845 in Dawes Court, off Shoe Lane by Fleet Street; her father, Edward Walker, was a locksmith and later a blacksmith.
Married William Nichols, a printer's machinist, at St Bride's in Fleet Street on 16 January 1864. They had five children: Edward, Percy, Alice, Eliza and Henry.
They lived for a time in the Peabody Buildings in Stamford Street. The marriage broke up in 1880, and Polly passed through the Lambeth workhouse more than once.
In the spring of 1888 she went into service with a respectable family in Wandsworth, and wrote to her father that she was settled in her new place; by July she had left it.

That August she lodged in Thrawl Street and then at the White House in Flower and Dean Street. On her last night she had spent her doss money three times over, and was proud of a new black straw bonnet.
She was buried on 6 September 1888 in the City of London Cemetery at Ilford. Her father and her eldest son came.

Born Eliza Ann Smith in Paddington in 1840, the daughter of George Smith, a soldier in the Life Guards, and his wife Ruth.
Married John Chapman, a coachman, in 1869. They lived in the West End and then at Windsor, where he drove for a gentleman. They had three children: Emily, Annie and John.
Emily died of meningitis in 1882 at twelve years old. Not long after, Annie and John parted; he sent her ten shillings a week by post until he died at Christmas, 1886.
In Spitalfields she made crochet work for antimacassars and sold it, with flowers and matches, and lodged at Crossingham's in Dorset Street. She was ill that summer, with a disease of the lungs.
On her last night she lacked the eightpence for her bed, and told the deputy not to let it, she would not be long.
She was buried on 14 September 1888 at Manor Park Cemetery. Her family paid for the funeral and kept it quiet.

Born Elisabeth Gustafsdotter on 27 November 1843 on a farm at Torslanda, near Gothenburg, in Sweden.
She came to London in 1866, and in 1869 married John Thomas Stride, a carpenter. Together they kept a coffee-room in Poplar.
She spoke Swedish and English, and went to the Swedish Church in Princes Square, which helped her when times were hard.

In her last years she lived with Michael Kidney, a waterside labourer, and earned what she could by cleaning and sewing. The day before she died she cleaned rooms at her lodging-house in Flower and Dean Street for sixpence.
That Saturday night she had pinned a red rose, backed with maidenhair fern, to her jacket.
She was buried on 6 October 1888 in the East London Cemetery at Plaistow, in a pauper's grave.

Born on 14 April 1842 at Graisley Green in Wolverhampton, the daughter of George Eddowes, a tinplate worker. The family moved to Bermondsey when she was a baby.

Her mother died in 1855 and her father two years later. She went back to Wolverhampton to her aunt, and later took up with Thomas Conway, an old soldier; she had his initials, TC, pricked in blue ink on her arm.
They had three children: Annie, Thomas and George. They walked the Midlands selling the ballads he printed.

From about 1881 she lived with John Kelly, a labourer, at Cooney's lodging-house in Flower and Dean Street. That September they went hop-picking in Kent, and walked back to London on the 28th with no money.
On the Saturday night she was taken to Bishopsgate police station for being drunk in Aldgate High Street, and let go at about one in the morning.
She was buried on 8 October 1888 in the City of London Cemetery at Ilford. Thousands lined the streets; the undertaker gave his work for nothing.
No. 13 Miller's Court, off Dorset Street
She told Joseph Barnett she was born in Limerick in about 1863 and grew up in Wales, where her father worked at an ironworks.
At sixteen she married a collier named Davies, who was killed in a pit explosion two or three years later.
She went to Cardiff, and then to London in about 1884. She liked to be called Marie Jeanette, and said she had once gone to France.
From 1887 she lived with Joseph Barnett, a porter at Billingsgate fish market, and from early 1888 in one room at No. 13 Miller's Court, rented from John McCarthy at 4s 6d a week.
On her last evening a neighbour heard her singing an old song, 'A Violet from Mother's Grave'.
She was buried on 19 November 1888 in St Patrick's Catholic Cemetery at Leytonstone. The sexton of St Leonard's, Shoreditch, paid for the funeral, and great crowds stood bareheaded as she passed.

Christ Church, Spitalfields: built 1714 to 1729 to Nicholas Hawksmoor's design, under the Act for Fifty New Churches. Its spire rises about two hundred feet over the market and the lodging-houses.

The Huguenot silk-weavers who fled France in the 1680s built the tall houses round it, with long garret windows to give light to the looms. By 1888 the weavers are mostly gone and the houses are let by the room.
Spitalfields Market, chartered in 1682 for fruit, vegetables and flowers. Mr Robert Horner, who had been a porter here, took the lease in 1875 and is putting up new market buildings.
The carts come in from Essex and Kent from midnight; by three in the morning the porters are running.
A common lodging-house: fourpence for a single bed for one night, eightpence for a double, the money paid each night before you go up. The kitchen and its fire are shared, and anyone may cook there.
In 1888 about eight and a half thousand people slept every night in the lodging-houses of Whitechapel and Spitalfields. Flower and Dean Street, a short street, had dozens of them.
The Ten Bells, a public house since the 1750s, on the corner of Commercial Street and Church Street, opposite Christ Church. The market men drink here from dawn.

Toynbee Hall, opened on Christmas Eve 1884 by the Reverend Samuel Barnett, vicar of St Jude's next door, and his wife Henrietta. Young university men live here among their neighbours, and teach, debate, run clubs and a library, and give free legal advice.
The Whitechapel Bell Foundry has stood on this spot since 1738. Here George Mears cast Big Ben in 1858 for the Clock Tower at Westminster, and here the Liberty Bell of Philadelphia was cast in 1752.

The Working Lads' Institute, opened in 1885 for the boys of Whitechapel: a gymnasium, baths, classes and a library. Its hall serves as the coroner's court for the district: the inquests on Mary Ann Nichols and Annie Chapman were held here, before Mr Wynne Baxter.

The London Hospital, founded in 1740 and here on the Whitechapel Road since 1757: the largest voluntary hospital in England, free to the poor, kept by gifts. Its Receiving Room takes the whole East End's accidents, day and night.

The Crown, at 74 Mile End Road. In an upstairs room on 10 September 1888, local tradesmen formed the Mile End Vigilance Committee, with Mr George Lusk, a builder, as its chairman, to patrol the streets, raise a reward, and press the Home Office.

Leman Street police station: the headquarters of H Division of the Metropolitan Police, which keeps Whitechapel. Inspector Edmund Reid heads its detectives; Inspector Frederick Abberline, who knew the district for fourteen years, has been sent back from Scotland Yard to lead the inquiry on the ground.

The Aldgate pump, at the meeting of Aldgate, Leadenhall Street and Fenchurch Street, the old edge of the City of London. Its water came from a deep well. 'East of Aldgate pump' is what Londoners call the East End.

Mitre Square, in the City of London (and so the City Police's ground, not the Metropolitan's). Kearley and Tonge's tea warehouses fill two sides; three dark ways lead in: Mitre Street, St James's Passage and Church Passage from Duke Street.
The Wentworth Model Dwellings, Goulston Street: new blocks of flats for working families, built by a charitable company, most of the tenants Jewish.
Buck's Row: a narrow cobbled street behind the Whitechapel Road, with Essex Wharf, the Board School, a row of cottages and Brown's stable yard. One gas lamp, at the far end.

Berner Street, off the Commercial Road: small houses, a Board School, and at No. 40 the International Working Men's Educational Club, a club of Jewish working men, mostly socialists, who meet to debate, sing and put out a Yiddish newspaper, Der Arbeter Fraint.

Dorset Street, between Commercial Street and Crispin Street: about a hundred and fifty yards of common lodging-houses and furnished rooms let by the night. John McCarthy, the chandler at No. 27, lets the rooms in Miller's Court behind.
The Star, the new halfpenny evening paper, first published on 17 January 1888 by T. P. O'Connor. It is loud and Radical, and it sold more copies over the murders than any paper before it.
The Paragon Theatre of Varieties, Mile End Road, opened in 1885: comic singers, acrobats, a chairman with a gavel, sixpence in the gallery.
A pillar box, painted red since 1874. Six collections a day in the East End.
A gas lamp: one every forty or fifty yards, if that, in the back streets, lit at dusk by the lamplighter with his pole. The courts and yards have none at all.
